steps.say: Counting those tiles IS finding the area: four in a row, three rows, 4 × 3 = 12. Area of a rectangle is just length × width.

That trip round the edge is the perimeter: add every side, 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 = 14, the same as 2 × (4 + 3). Area fills the inside (multiply); perimeter goes round the edge (add). Those two ideas run through every question here. Algebra just calls the sides \(l\) and \(w\): area \(= l \times w\), perimeter \(= 2(l + w)\).

method_card.title: How to Find Area & Perimeter
method_card.content:
Key area formulas:

$$\text{Rectangle} = l \times w \qquad \text{Triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times b \times h \qquad \text{Parallelogram} = b \times h$$

$$\text{Trapezium} = \frac{1}{2}(a + b) \times h \qquad \text{Circle} = \pi r^2 \qquad \text{Circumference} = 2\pi r = \pi d$$

For compound shapes, split into simpler shapes and add (or subtract) their areas. Always use the perpendicular height, not the slant height.
method_card.example:
Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm and height 4 cm.

\(A = \frac{1}{2}(6 + 10) \times 4 = \frac{1}{2} \times 16 \times 4 = 32\) cm²

steps: Gold questions combine steps, often with sectors, rings, or a mix of straight and curved edges.
Work in stages and keep full accuracy on your calculator until the very end. Rounding partway (say a circle's circumference) can push the final answer out by a whole unit.
A sector or arc is a fraction \(\tfrac{\theta}{360}\) of the whole circle; a ring is the big area minus the small area (square each radius first).
gold.title: Gold: several steps chained

example.question: A sector has radius 8 cm and angle 135°. Find the area (1 d.p.).

steps: Pick the shape and its formula. Rectangle area is \(l \times w\); triangle is \(\tfrac{1}{2}bh\); parallelogram is \(b \times h\); trapezium is \(\tfrac{1}{2}(a+b)h\).
Put the numbers straight in and calculate. Do not muddle area with perimeter: area multiplies (units cm²); perimeter adds the sides (units cm).
For circles, circumference is \(\pi d\) and area is \(\pi r^2\). Square the radius before multiplying by \(\pi\).

steps: The formula will not take the numbers as given, so do one preparation step first.
Common preparations: halve a diameter to get the radius; take a fraction of a circle (half, quarter); rearrange a formula to find a missing length; or split a compound shape into rectangles and add.
Then finish as in bronze, and check by working back to a number you were given.

misconceptions.message: It looks like you stopped at the radius squared. Take the square root: r = √(50.3 ÷ π) ≈ √16 = 4.0 cm.
